items.claim: A front-channel GET to the /authorization endpoint carrying response_type=code, followed by a redirect of the user to the registered redirect_uri after consent, is how a hunter confirms the client is using the authorization code grant and captures the endpoints to attack.
items.body:
A front-channel GET to the /authorization endpoint carrying response_type=code, followed by a redirect of the user to the registered redirect_uri after consent, is how a hunter confirms the client is using the authorization code grant and captures the endpoints to attack.

HackTricks reference: oauth 2.0 hunting methodology (https://kathan19.gitbook.io/howtohunt/oauth/oauth-2.0-hunting-methodology.md)
items.disproof: If the authorization request uses a different response_type, or no /authorization request and provider redirect are captured at all, this flow signature does not identify the grant in use.

sources.quote:
GET /authorization?client_id=12345&redirect_uri=https://client-app.com/callback&response_type=code&scope=openid%20profile&state=ae13d489bd00e3c24 HTTP/1.1 
Host: oauth-authorization-server.com


* So, in authorization code grant type the response_type parameter should be code . this code is used to request access token from the oauth service.
* Now, after the user login to their account with the OAuth provider and gives consent to access their data. the user will be redirected to the /callback endpoint that was specified in the redirect_uri parameter of the authorization request.

The complexity of implementing and managing pattern matching correctly obviously causes security issues. This document therefore advises simplifying the required logic and configuration by using exact redirection URI matching.

items.claim: In the authorization code grant the credential is handed over in the front-channel redirect, arriving as a query parameter on the redirect_uri, so it is visible in proxy history and server logs rather than kept server-side.

items.claim: Only the front-channel legs of the authorization code flow appear in the proxy: the code-for-access-token exchange and the subsequent API calls run back-end and are never observed, so the flow must be identified from response_type=code plus an authorization code parameter on the /callback request.
items.body:

items.claim: Base64 in a SAML message is an encoding and not a protection, so a captured assertion decodes in one step and exposes the identity claims it carries for tampering analysis.
items.body:
Base64 in a SAML message is an encoding and not a protection, so a captured assertion decodes in one step and exposes the identity claims it carries for tampering analysis.

HackTricks reference: saml (https://kathan19.gitbook.io/howtohunt/saml/saml.md)
items.disproof: An assertion that is genuinely encrypted rather than base64-encoded, or a capture that never exposes the message, cannot be read by decoding it.

sources.quote:
Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) is one of the ways one can implement SSO.
* Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) is a markup language implemented in XML.
* SAML messages are base64 encoded but that is easily decoded to view the message contents.
* SAML and OAuth are different protocols and are used for different purposes, OAuth is a protocol for authorization while SAML is a protocol for authentication.
